SK2210 The constant index or range cannot be valid

A constant index or range that no collection length can make valid, so the element access throws for every input.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperNegativeIndex (resharper_negative_index_highlighting)

Why

Three shapes, and what they have in common is that the length never enters the arithmetic. x[^0] is one past the end whatever x holds — ^0 is Length - 0, not the last element — and it throws on a full collection and an empty one alike; it is the language wart that catches everyone once, and ^1 is what was meant. A range whose start is fixed above its end, x[3..1] or x[^1..^3], is rejected by Range.GetOffsetAndLength before any length is consulted. A negative constant index throws from every positional indexer. ⚠ This is not SK2001 and not SK2053. SK2001 folds a comparison the operand type's range decides and SK2053 one a count's non-negativity decides; neither looks at an element access at all, and no type range or count contract says anything about ^0. The fact this rule adds is the indexing contract itself: the offset ^0 denotes, the ordering Range requires of its endpoints, and the non-negativity every positional indexer requires of its argument — each provable from the constants on the page with no knowledge of the length whatsoever. There is no fix, for SK2001's reason: the rule can prove the access throws and cannot know whether ^1, 1..3 or 0 was intended.

Example

Instead of:

var last = values[^0];

Write:

var last = values[^1];

When it does not fire

⚠ `^0` is only reported where it indexes an element, never where it bounds a range. x[..^0] is the whole collection and x[^0..] is an empty slice; both are legal, both are measured to be legal on an empty collection too, and a rule that folded them in with x[^0] would report the two spellings people use deliberately. The distinction is the syntactic parent: an index argument of an element access is reported, an endpoint of a range expression is not. ⚠ A reversed range is reported only where both endpoints are constants of the same kind. a..b compares directly and ^a..^b compares the other way round — the start is Length - a and the end is Length - b, so it is invalid exactly when b > a. A mixed 3..^1 and a range with an omitted endpoint depend on the length and are declined. 2..2 and ^3..^1 are empty and forward respectively, and neither is reported. ⚠ A negative constant index is declined on arrays, because `CS0251` already owns them, and it is measured rather than assumed: the compiler reports a[-1] on an array and stays silent on "abc"[-1], list[-1] and span[-1], which all throw at run time. The receiver must be a string, a Span, a ReadOnlySpan, a Memory, a ReadOnlyMemory or a type implementing IList, IList<T> or IReadOnlyList<T> whose indexer takes a single int; a dictionary is excluded outright, since map[-1] is an ordinary key lookup and not an out-of-range access. A user-defined indexer outside those contracts is free to give a negative argument any meaning it likes and is never reported. Generated code is excluded.
